Components of a battery
 Anode :  Oxidation takes place
                     Electroactive material : metals which can undergo oxidation easily

                    Electroactive material : compounds which can undergo reduction easily
                     PbO2, MnO2, O2

                        H2SO4, KOH, Nafion

                       Role -  To prevent internal short circuit 
                       Transport ions from anode to cathode compartments and vice versa 
                       Polypropylene, Cellophane

Based on working, two types of batteries:
Primary battery
Electroactive material cannot be regenerated
Discarded after electroactive species is consumed
Galvanic cell
Dry cell, Li-MnO2

Secondary battery
Electroactive material can be regenerated
Can be used several times
Galvanic as well as electrolytic cell
Storage battery

Reserve  batteries

One of the key component is kept separated from the rest of the battery and
 Is allowed to come in contact with other components when required
 Usually the electrolyte is the component that is isolated
  This prevents chemical reaction between the cell components (self discharge)
   Has unlimited shelf life
   Usually designed for emergency use e.g mid-air crisis
Examples: Mg-AgCl(water activated) , Zn-Ag2O(KOH activated)
Applications: Sonobuoys, Weather balloons, Emergency lights etc.,

Energy Storage Devices

Electricity Storage density: 
 Amount of charge or electricity per unit weight which the battery can hold
            ESD= Capacity/ Weight of the battery
Weight includes weight of all the components of the battery - electrodes, electrolyte, case, current collectors, terminals etc 
To get high  electricity storage density, use of right kind of material for all the components is important
e.g.,  7g of Li is required at anode to give 1F of charge whereas 104g of Pb is required for the same amount of charge

 Corrosion at contact points 

 Shedding of active material from the plates

 Shorting between electrodes due to irregular crystal 
  growth and changes in morphology

Source slide page 9 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Lithium  batteries

Lithium is a popular anodic material:
Light weight metal. The electrochemical equivalence of lithium is high (7g of lithium can give 1F of charge)
High negative standard reduction potential of -3.05V ; when  coupled with other electrodes gives high voltage
        ( about 4V)
Aqueous electrolytes cannot be used as Lithium is  very reactive and it reacts vigorously with water . So organic and inorganic electrolytes are used

Energy Storage Devices

Components of Lithium batteries: Lithium is used as anode; Cathode can be MnO2, SO2Cl2. Electrolyte can be Li salt in organic solvents like acetonitrile, propylene carbonate or inorganic solvents like SOCl2 
Types of Lithium batteries : 
Primary batteries which are not rechargeable, e.g.  Li-MnO2 
Secondary batteries which are rechargeable, e.g. Solid state lithium metal battery

Advantages of lithium batteries
 High Voltage up to 4V
 High energy density – Lightest metal
 High tolerance to service conditions  (-40 oC to 70 oC) 
 High electricity storage density
 Flat discharge characteristics

Disadvantages of lithium batteries
 Safety concerns due to high reactivity of Lithium metal 
 Poor cycle life – due to dendrite formation
 Transportation limit

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Lithium-ion battery (Lithium iron phosphate as cathode)
Principle :
  Lithium ion moves from anode to cathode while discharging and from cathode to anode while charging
  Materials used as anode and cathode should be capable of lodging  Lithium ions
  Anode material: Lithiated graphite        
 Cathodic material : Lithium Iron phosphate

Source slide page 4 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Construction

Component | Material | Function

Anode (negative electrode) | Graphite, C₆ | Stores lithium ions during charging

Cathode (positive electrode) | Lithium iron phosphate, LiFePO₄ | Source and host of lithium ions

Electrolyte | Lithium salt such as LiPF₆ dissolved in organic carbonate solvents | Conducts Li⁺ ions between electrodes

Separator | Microporous polymer, commonly polyethylene (PE) or polypropylene (PP) | Prevents direct electrical contact while allowing Li⁺ transport

Current collector—anode | Copper (Cu) foil | Conducts electrons from/to the graphite electrode

Current collector—cathode | Aluminium (Al) foil | Conducts electrons from/to the LiFePO₄ electrode

Cell casing | Steel, aluminium, or polymer pouch | Provides mechanical protection

POTENTIOMETRIC SENSORS
These sensors detect changes in the concentration of a substance by observing how the concentration changes the electrical potential produced by a redox reaction at the electrode.
The redox reaction takes place on the electrode surface:

It measures the potential difference (voltage) between an indicator electrode and a reference electrode under conditions of negligible current flow, and relates this potential to the activity or concentration of a specific ion or analyte in a solution.

Working of Glucose Biosensor
Developed by Updike and Hicks 
Enzyme Glucose oxidase(GOx) catalyze the oxidation of glucose by molecular oxygen producing glucolactone and hydrogen peroxide.
In order to work as a catalyst, GOx requires a redox cofactor –flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), works as an initial electron acceptor and is reduced to FADH2. 
Glucose + GOx –FAD   Glucolactone + GOx – FADH2

Working of Glucose Biosensor

The cofactor is regenerated by reacting with oxygen, leading to the formation of hydrogen peroxide 
GOx – FADH2 + O2   GOx – FAD + H2O2 
 Hydrogen peroxide is oxidized at a platinum electrode. 
The number of electron transfers, at electrode surface is directly proportional to the number of glucose molecules present in the blood. 
H2O2  2H+ +O2 + 2e-

Principle Features and Content e)

1. Prevent Waste The primary goal is to synthesize the target product with little to no by-
products or waste. Waste treatment adds to costs.

2. Atom Economy Maximize the incorporation of reactants into the final product. Aim for 100%
atom economy using addition/rearrangement reactions.

3. Safer Synthesis Minimize or avoid hazardous substances in synthesis. Example: Use CO,
instead of toxic phosgene in polyurethane synthesis.

4. Safe Products Products should be effective but with reduced toxicity. Minimize harmful side
effects on users and the environment.

5. Design Benign Chemicals Use safer solvents/reaction conditions. Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform;
prefer water, CO,, ionic liquids, or solvent-free systems.

6. Design for Energy Efficiency Reduce energy intensity by using catalysts (e.g., bio-catalysts) and modern
methods like microwave or ultrasound irradiation.

7. Use of Renewable Feedstock Prefer renewable raw materials like biomass over non-renewable sources
such as coal and petroleum.

8. Reduce Derivatives Avoid unnecessary derivatization steps (e.g., blocking/protecting groups) to
minimize waste and enhance atom efficiency.

9. Catalysis Use catalysts to accelerate reactions, reduce energy use, and achieve high
yields with recyclable, selective reactions.

10. Design for Degradation Products should degrade into harmless substances after use to prevent
environmental accumulation (e.g., pesticides, polymers).

11. Pollution Prevention Employ real-time monitoring and control of processes to prevent hazardous
substances. Recycle unreacted chemicals.

12. Accident Prevention Choose chemicals and processes to minimize risks of accidents like fires,
explosions, and toxic releases. Equip facilities with safety measures.
